title: NVLink multi-GPU kernel routing: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM performance deep dive
summary: Deep technical profiling of an 8x A100 NVLink cluster comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths. We focused on kernel selection, CUDA graph capture/fallback stability, KV-cache sharding and prefetching across NVLink islands, batching strategies (static vs dynamic), quantization artifacts (fp16 vs int8), and networking/VPC considerations for pinned GPU affinity. Agreed next steps include sharing traces, running a persistent KV-cache run, and setting up an on-site VPC diagram review.
topics: CUDA Graph capture and fallback behavior

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-10
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Solutions), Priya (AeroCloud Infra), Miguel (AeroCloud ML), Ben (AeroCloud CTO)

Summary (auto): deep-dive on multi-gpu nvlink perf comparing trt-llm and vllm, focusing on kernel selection, cuda-graph capture stability and kv-cache behavior across devices.

00:00 Alex: okay folks, thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda - show traces we captured, point out where kernel routing differs, then discuss kv-cache sharding and network implications.
00:12 Priya: thanks. our priority is p99 stability for synchronous requests and keeping tail latency < 250ms for short chats. we run an 8x A100 NVLink cluster, mixed 2k/8k contexts.
00:25 Samira: great, i'll start with the nvprof trace from yesterday - mixed workload, about 60% long contexts. the first thing i noticed was different kernel selection at the attention and feedforward ops between trt-llm and vllm.
00:38 Samira: (screen share ref: tinyurl.com/redwood-traces) in trt-llm we see fused attention kernels that reduce launch overhead but sometimes block on a cross-gpu collective when the attention slices span nvlink islands, that part increases p99.
00:55 Miguel: small question - when you say "nvlink islands" you mean the way our 8 cards are topologically connected, right? we have two x4 bridged groups on the board.
01:02 Samira: yes exactly, so if your context and kv mapping cause attention KV to hop across islands, you hit cross-link latency. vllm's path tends to use many smaller kernels with more async overlap which sometimes helps hide that link cost, but it increases kernel launch overhead.
01:20 Ben: is that consistent across fp16 and int8? our plan is to try int8 quant for cost, but don't want stability regressions.
01:29 Samira: so on int8 we saw reduced compute time but more numerical variance in softmax and occasional decoding artifacts; also int8 kernels in trt-llm are more fused and can exacerbate the cross-gpu wait if the whole fused op needs synchronized KV. in fp16, vllm sometimes wins p99 because it streams smaller kernels and leverages asynchronous copies.
01:50 Alex: to add, we saw cuda-graph capture interactions too. trt-llm attempts to capture large graphs which helps throughput, but if the runtime falls back (e.g., dynamic sequence lengths), the fallback path causes a large latency spike. vllm's execution is less reliant on big cuda-graphs so it's more stable for mixed-length traffic.
02:08 Miguel: we recorded an incident where cuda-graph failed and all requests spiked - do you have a recommended guardrail?
02:15 Samira: yes, two immediate mitigations: enable conservative graph capture (smaller capture windows) and configure automatic fallback threshold lower so it falls back earlier but more gracefully. Redwood's runtime also supports hybrid mode where small batches use non-graph path and large batches use graph path. we can share exact config.
02:31 Priya: about KV-cache - how does sharding work across devices? we care about eviction and prefetching.
02:38 Jordan: good callout. in our experiments the KV cache is sharded round-robin across GPUs by default to balance memory; however for NVLink setups we recommend affinity sharding: colocate KV for frequently accessed prefixes on the same NVLink island as the compute to minimize cross-link traffic.
02:55 Miguel: that sounds tricky to implement. do you have automation to remap shards based on hot prefixes?
03:02 Samira: yes - Redwood Optimize can profile token-hotness and suggest a remap. we also experimented with prefetching the top-k hot prefixes to the local GPU before generation bursts, which reduces p99 but increases memory pressure.
03:18 Ben: what's the memory tradeoff, approx how many tokens worth of KV would you prefetch?
03:24 Samira: in the test we prefetched 512 tokens-worth per hot prefix and that lowered cross-island traffic by about 35% for this workload but increased gpu memory by ~4GB per card. results vary.
03:38 Alex: moving to batching, we tested static big batches vs dynamic batching with a short-latency fast-lane. static gives higher throughput but p99 suffers for latency-sensitive requests. dynamic batching with a separate low-latency path (small batch size, prefer local KV) gave the best balance.
03:58 Miguel: does Redwood runtime support dual queues for low/high latency?
04:03 Jordan: yes, you can configure routing policies: prefer latency path (no cross-island sharding, small batch) for premium traffic; lower-priority traffic goes to high-throughput path that uses larger graph captures.
04:15 Priya: network/VPC side - if we deploy private on-prem or VPC-connected hosts, are there constraints for pinning GPUs and ensuring NVLink affinity?
04:24 Samira: for on-prem you have full control, but in VPC the critical bit is ensuring your host topology maps to physical GPU pairs. Redwood Private can expose a pinning API so dedicated pods hang on to specific GPU sets; for cloud-hosted you need provider support to guarantee NVLink topology.
04:40 Ben: we use a cloud bare-metal partner; they said they can provide physical adjacency but we have to route within the VPC. any network configs to watch?
04:49 Samira: ensure low-latency fabric between hosts for KV synchronization, and avoid over-subscribed NICs for control plane traffic. also use private link and jumbo frames where possible. we'll send a checklist.
05:02 Alex: i want to highlight an oddity in one of the traces: around minute 43 of the capture a cuda-graph failed to replay and the runtime retried with smaller capture window but we saw double alloc/free churn causing a memory spike - that's likely the customer's workload switching between 2k and 8k contexts rapidly.
05:23 Miguel: that matches our mixed workload pattern. any recommendation to smooth that?
05:27 Samira: yes, set a threshold to treat <1.5k sequences as small-path and >1.5k as graphable; plus enable persistent KV cache to avoid reallocation on warm-starts. persistent KV cache reduced alloc churn in our tests.
05:42 Priya: curious about performance delta numbers - can you provide p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec comparisons for our traces?
05:49 Alex: yes, summary numbers we ran: trt-llm throughput 1.3x vllm for large-batch steady-state, but vllm had 20-40% lower p99 on mixed small-batch traffic. int8 gave 1.6x compute speedup but introduced decoding variance in ~2% of sequences on our sample.
06:10 Ben: that's helpful. for a production pilot we prefer predictable p99 over absolute throughput. our question: is it worth dedicating NVLink pinned pairs and using vllm to get stable p99, or use trt-llm with careful capture tuning?
06:22 Samira: both are viable. tradeoffs: trt-llm + aggressive graph capture = best throughput and lower cost per token but higher operational overhead to tune capture and avoid fallbacks; vllm = simpler, more stable tail latency but higher token cost. Dedicated pinned NVLink pairs + affinity sharding helps either approach.
06:44 Alex: ok, recap and next steps - we'll upload traces and a benchmark spreadsheet, Samira will run the persistent KV-cache 8xA100 trace and send CSVs, Priya will share VPC topology. follow-up next week to review.
06:58 Priya: thanks everyone, appreciate the depth.
07:02 Meeting end.
